items.title: How We Built an MCP Server on Our Existing APIs
items.summary: We built an MCP server for our product in a few weeks. Most of it was reuse: the same reporting APIs, the same identity provider, the same Kubernetes cluster and pipeline. Kubernetes: one more subchart in the existing Helm release, in the same cluster and namespace as the APIs. It calls them by internal service name, so tool traffic stays inside the cluster. Ingress: new routes on the existing gateway for /mcp and the well known discovery paths. The server runs on the tenant's existing host name. More tools, based on what customers actually ask. Write actions that only draft a change for a person to approve. Usage telemetry on which tools and questions get used. If you already have secure APIs and an identity provider, you don't need a new platform to get started. A thin MCP server on top of them is enough for version 1. items.summary_html:
We built an MCP server for our product in a few weeks. Most of it was reuse: the same reporting APIs, the same identity provider, the same Kubernetes cluster and pipeline. This is a write up of what we did, what worked and what we plan next.

Why

Our customers have a lot of operational data in our product: orders, events, exceptions, team and location performance. Today they see it through report screens. When they have a question the screens don't answer, it becomes a feature request or an Excel export.

Most of our customers already use an AI assistant. So the ask was: let them connect their own assistant to their data in our product, with the same permissions they have in the web app. No new copy of the data, no new login.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Today
        Q1[New question] --> F1[Feature request] --> F2[Report built
weeks later] --> F3[Answer]
        Q1 --> E1[Export to
Excel] --> F3
    end
    subgraph With MCP
        Q2[Question in
plain language] --> AI[AI assistant] --> T[MCP tools] --> A2[Answer and chart]
    end
What MCP is

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to other systems. A server exposes tools. Each tool has a name, typed inputs and a description. The assistant reads the descriptions, decides which tools to call and uses the results in its answer. Since it is a standard, one server works with Claude, other assistants, IDEs and the customer's own agents.

flowchart LR
    C1[Claude] --> S
    C2[Other AI assistants] --> S
    C3[IDE and agent tools] --> S
    C4[Customer's own agent] --> S
    S[MCP server] --> P[(Operational data)]

We looked at two other options before choosing MCP:

Option Why not Build our own chatbot We would own the model, the UI and the cost. Customers already have assistants. Export data to a warehouse for AI New pipelines, stale data, a second permission model and a bigger security review. MCP server Chosen. Works with any assistant and uses our existing security.
Where the tools get data

There were three choices:

  1. A new data API built for AI.
  2. A warehouse or lakehouse loaded with reporting data.
  3. The reporting APIs our web app already uses.

We went with the third. The reporting service already finds the tenant for each request and connects to that tenant's database, checks the user's permissions on every endpoint and reads through stored procedures that are tuned and tested.

flowchart TB
    Q{Where should the
tools get data?}
    Q --> N[New data API]
    Q --> W[Warehouse or lakehouse]
    Q --> E[Existing reporting APIs]
    N --> N1[Duplicate tenancy,
auth and queries]
    W --> W1[New pipelines,
new permission model]
    E --> E1[Tenancy, permissions and
queries already exist]
    E1 --> OK[Chosen for version 1]
    W1 -. "later, for analytics" .-> LT[See: Next phase]

So the MCP server only translates. A tool call comes in, it calls an existing endpoint and returns a compact JSON result. It has no database credentials. If a user can't see something in the web app, the assistant can't see it either.

Architecture 
flowchart LR
    U[User] --> A[AI assistant
any MCP client]
    A -- "MCP over HTTPS
+ user's access token" --> G[Ingress /
API gateway]
    G --> M[MCP server
stateless container]
    M -- "same token
+ tenant header" --> R[Existing reporting API]
    M -- "same token" --> O[Existing app API
e.g. location list]
    R --> D[(Tenant reporting
database)]
    A -. "OAuth sign in" .-> I[Existing identity
provider]
    M -. "verify token
signature" .-> I
  • AI assistant: any MCP client. We used Claude with a custom connector.
  • MCP server: a small TypeScript service on the official MCP SDK. It defines the tools, validates inputs, calls the APIs and trims the results.
  • Identity provider: our existing OpenID Connect provider, same one the web app uses.
  • Reporting API and database: no changes, except two new endpoints (see Performance below).
Authentication

We expected this to be the hardest part. It was mostly configuration, because MCP uses standard OAuth.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as AI assistant
    participant M as MCP server
    participant I as Identity provider
    participant R as Reporting API

    C->>M: Call /mcp (no token)
    M-->>C: 401 + pointer to resource metadata
    C->>M: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
    M-->>C: "My authorization server is "
    C->>I: Discover endpoints, start sign in (PKCE)
    I-->>C: User signs in as usual, gets access token
    C->>M: Call tool with Bearer token
    M->>M: Verify signature and issuer
    M->>R: Same request, same token
    R-->>M: Data the user is allowed to see
    M-->>C: Compact result
  • Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728). For a request without a token, the server returns 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header. The header points to a small JSON document that tells the assistant which authorization server to use.
  • Authorization server metadata. Some clients look for discovery documents at specific well known paths, so we serve the identity provider's metadata at those paths too.
  • Authorization code flow with PKCE. The user signs in on the normal login page. PKCE secures the exchange without a client secret, since the assistant is a public client.
  • Token pass through. The server checks the token signature and issuer, then sends the same token to the APIs. The APIs enforce permissions the same way they do for the web app. The model never sees the token.
Public client instead of dynamic registration

MCP clients can register themselves with the identity provider automatically (dynamic client registration). Many enterprise identity setups don't allow that. Our first try failed with a generic "couldn't register" error. We created one public client for MCP, allowed only the assistant's redirect URL, and entered that client ID in the connector settings. That fixed it.

Token claims

Our APIs filter data using claims in the token, for example which locations a user can see and which roles they have. A new client doesn't get the same claims as the web app client by default, so we added the same claim mappers. Check this early. A valid token with a missing claim returns empty results, and it takes time to figure out why.

Multi tenancy

Each customer has its own subdomain and its own identity realm. The MCP server gets everything from the host name of the request:

  • the tenant, sent as a header to the APIs so they connect to the right database,
  • the expected token issuer, so a token from one tenant is rejected on another,
  • the resource metadata URL it advertises. 
flowchart LR
    H["Request host
customer-a.example.com"] --> P[MCP server parses host]
    P --> T1[Tenant id
customer-a]
    P --> T2[Expected issuer
customer-a realm]
    P --> T3[Resource metadata URL]
    T1 --> API[Tenant header on
every API call]
    API --> DB[(customer-a
reporting database)]
    T2 --> V{Token issuer
matches?}
    V -- no --> X[401 rejected]
    V -- yes --> API

One deployment serves all tenants on a cluster, with no per tenant configuration. Signing keys are fetched from each issuer and cached.

Tool design

Most of the answer quality depends on this.

  • Small set of read only tools. We started with eight, covering a location list, KPI summary, team and location performance, exceptions, slowest events and record lookup. No write actions in version 1.
  • Write descriptions for the model. Each description says what the tool returns, what each input means and when to use it. For example, the location input says to call the location list first if the user gives a city name. With that one line, users can say "Chicago" instead of an internal code.
  • Summarize on the server. API responses built for screens can be hundreds of KB. We aggregate before returning, for example totals per team instead of every event. One response went from over 700 KB to under 50 KB. Smaller results are faster, cost fewer tokens and give more accurate answers.
  • Limit the size. Top 10 by default and row caps on everything.
  • Validate inputs. Zod schemas reject bad dates or missing fields before any API call, with an error message the model can act on.
  • Ask for charts. MCP servers can send instructions to the client. Ours asks for a chart when the result compares items or shows a trend.

Example of one question turning into two tool calls. The model decides the order from the descriptions:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as AI assistant
    participant M as MCP server
    U->>A: "Where are the biggest delays at our Chicago site this month?"
    A->>M: list_locations(search: "Chicago")
    M-->>A: Chicago = location code CHI
    A->>M: get_slowest_events(location: CHI, from, to)
    M-->>A: Top 10 items with average delay minutes
    A-->>U: Bar chart + explanation + suggested actions
flowchart LR
    R[Raw API response
every record, every event
~700 KB] --> S[MCP server
aggregate, rank, top N] --> O[Tool result
per team totals
under 50 KB]
Performance

Two of our questions ("longest delays last month" and "exceptions by location") took several minutes in the first version. The queries were parsing large JSON event records across millions of rows on every call.

We fixed it with regular database work:

  • a summary table with one row per event and the duration and exception flags already calculated,
  • a stored procedure that refreshes it for a date range,
  • two small query stored procedures behind two new reporting endpoints. 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Before["Before: minutes"]
        Q1[Tool call] --> J[Parse JSON events
across millions of rows] --> A1[Answer]
    end
    subgraph After["After: under a second"]
        S[Scheduled refresh
stored procedure] --> T[(Event
summary table)]
        Q2[Tool call] --> P[Small query
stored procedure] --> T
        P --> A2[Answer]
    end

Both now return in under a second.

In our tests, the MCP server and APIs take about 0.1 to 2.5 seconds per tool call. Most of the remaining time is the model thinking and writing. A faster model, lower reasoning effort, simple charts and small results help more than tuning the server further.

Hosting

Nothing new was set up.

  • Container: a small multi stage Docker image.
  • Kubernetes: one more subchart in the existing Helm release, in the same cluster and namespace as the APIs. It calls them by internal service name, so tool traffic stays inside the cluster.
  • Ingress: new routes on the existing gateway for /mcp and the well known discovery paths. The server runs on the tenant's existing host name.
  • Stateless transport: MCP Streamable HTTP in stateless mode. Each request gets a new server and transport, so no sticky sessions and it scales horizontally.
  • CI/CD: the existing pipeline builds, scans and pushes the image with the other services. 
flowchart TB
    subgraph CI["CI/CD pipeline (existing)"]
        B[Build image] --> SC[Security scan] --> PU[Push to registry]
    end
    PU --> HL[Helm release
new subchart added]
    subgraph K["Kubernetes cluster (existing)"]
        IN[Ingress gateway
+ /mcp and well known routes] --> MS[MCP server pods
stateless]
        MS --> RS[Reporting API service]
        MS --> AS[App API service]
        IN --> WEB[Web app]
    end
    HL --> MS
    Internet[AI assistant] --> IN

Few things we ran into:

  • Our build installs all workspace packages at once. Adding the MCP server to the main backend workspace pushed a code analysis step over its memory limit. Moving it to its own folder fixed it.
  • After a deploy, the gateway can take a minute or more to pick up new pods. Run at least two replicas for anything you demo live.
  • Our database deployment is incremental and skips new tables, so the summary table needed a release script.
Connecting Claude

This took a few minutes:

  1. An org admin adds a custom connector with the MCP URL.
  2. In advanced settings, the admin sets our public client ID (no secret).
  3. Each user clicks Connect and signs in on the normal login page. 
flowchart LR
    A1[Admin adds custom
connector with MCP URL] --> A2[Admin sets public
client id, no secret]
    A2 --> U1[User clicks Connect]
    U1 --> U2[Normal login page]
    U2 --> U3[Tools available in chat]

After that, a user can ask "How did the Chicago site do last Monday? Show it as a dashboard" and get the answer with charts.

What we learned
  1. The existing APIs already handled tenancy and permissions. That is why the MCP server is only a few hundred lines.
  2. Standard OAuth was enough. Resource metadata, PKCE and a public client worked with our identity provider without custom auth code.
  3. Tool descriptions, result size and defaults matter more than the number of tools.
  4. If a question is slow in SQL, it is slower through an assistant. Precompute it.
  5. Treat a live demo like a release: sign in beforehand, two replicas, and questions that return in seconds.
Other next steps
  • Finer scopes, so a customer can give the assistant less access than the full user has.
  • Audience restriction on tokens issued for the MCP client.
  • More tools, based on what customers actually ask.
  • Write actions that only draft a change for a person to approve.
  • Usage telemetry on which tools and questions get used.

If you already have secure APIs and an identity provider, you don't need a new platform to get started. A thin MCP server on top of them is enough for version 1. See what people ask, then decide what to build behind it.

items.title: Why Generated SQL Is Never Auto-Executed
items.summary: Quick answer: The modeling package has no executing driver. Every DDL, index, and deployment script is generated for review, and the software cannot run it against the database itself. The deployment script is idempotent and forward-only, so a person confirms each change before it is applied. This keeps a proposed migration from reaching the storage without a review. Why auto-execution is the wrong default A generated migration can look complete while carrying an assumption the reviewer should catch. An inferred link table, an open question, or a field diff that touches a shared table all need a decision, and running the SQL the moment it is generated would remove the pause where that decision happens. The blast radius of a schema change is large and hard to reverse, so the default should favor review rather than speed. Keeping the executing driver out of the package enforces that boundary in the tooling rather than relying on discipline alone. What the package can and cannot do Capability Available? Generate DDL and indexes Yes Generate deterministic seed data Yes Write deployment scripts Yes Execute writes or DDL No Execute a driver against the database No The same package that produces the SQL deliberately lacks the ability to run it, so there is no hidden path where a generated change reaches the storage unconfirmed. How a change actually reaches the database Review the four-layer reconciliation and the table status. Read the field diffs and the impacted operations. Resolve the open questions and confirm the inferred items. Review the generated SQL and the forward-only deployment script. Apply the change through your own controlled process. The script is idempotent, so running it more than once does not produce duplicate changes, and forward-only means it moves the schema ahead rather than reversing earlier migrations. Those properties make the reviewed script safe to run, but the decision to run it stays with the team. Picture a migration that adds a link table and a foreign key. The generated SQL is complete and internally consistent, but the link table is inferred from a relationship the business rules actually treat as one-to-many, and the open question is still attached. If the package could execute the script, the wrong join table would be created before anyone reads the note. With the executing driver absent, the reviewer opens the inference, resolves the cardinality, and only then runs the corrected script. The same protection catches a field diff that touches a shared table, because the pause is where the impacted operations get checked. This does not slow the happy path much, since a fully reviewed script still runs in one controlled step, but it removes the path where a confident-looking migration reaches the storage unconfirmed. How this fits the safety model This is the same boundary that keeps read-only access and static signals honest. The tool can read a live database through a saved profile and generate precise SQL, but it does not write, and a read-only SELECT is the only query the data layer runs. Writes and DDL are blocked at the connection layer. Treat the generated SQL as a detailed proposal, not a pending action, and keep the execution step separate and deliberate. A script that cannot be triggered automatically cannot be triggered by accident. Powerduck keeps the review and the execution separate by design, so every schema change is confirmed before it touches the storage. Frequently asked questions Can the tool run the migration for me? No. The modeling package has no executing driver, and SQL is generated for review. What makes the deployment script safe to run? It is idempotent and forward-only, so it avoids duplicate changes and does not reverse earlier migrations. Are writes blocked entirely? The data layer runs only a read-only SELECT, and writes and DDL are blocked. The bottom line The generated SQL is a reviewed artifact, not an executed action. With no executing driver in the package, every DDL and migration waits for a person to confirm it, and the idempotent, forward-only script makes the eventual run safe without making it automatic. This keeps a hard-to-reverse schema change from reaching the storage by accident. The line between generating and executing is the core safety control.

The same protection catches a field diff that touches a shared table, because the pause is where the impacted operations get checked. This does not slow the happy path much, since a fully reviewed script still runs in one controlled step, but it removes the path where a confident-looking migration reaches the storage unconfirmed.

How this fits the safety model

This is the same boundary that keeps read-only access and static signals honest. The tool can read a live database through a saved profile and generate precise SQL, but it does not write, and a read-only SELECT is the only query the data layer runs. Writes and DDL are blocked at the connection layer.

Treat the generated SQL as a detailed proposal, not a pending action, and keep the execution step separate and deliberate. A script that cannot be triggered automatically cannot be triggered by accident.

Powerduck keeps the review and the execution separate by design, so every schema change is confirmed before it touches the storage.

Frequently asked questions

Can the tool run the migration for me? No. The modeling package has no executing driver, and SQL is generated for review.

What makes the deployment script safe to run? It is idempotent and forward-only, so it avoids duplicate changes and does not reverse earlier migrations.

Are writes blocked entirely? The data layer runs only a read-only SELECT, and writes and DDL are blocked.

The bottom line

The generated SQL is a reviewed artifact, not an executed action. With no executing driver in the package, every DDL and migration waits for a person to confirm it, and the idempotent, forward-only script makes the eventual run safe without making it automatic. This keeps a hard-to-reverse schema change from reaching the storage by accident. The line between generating and executing is the core safety control. Read more in the API data model guide.

Pulse Hz와 Pulse depth로 리듬을 조절할 수 있습니다. 양안 융합 (Magenta Focus Cue) : 약시안 화면에는 고가시성 마젠타 핑크 원형 단서가, 우세안 화면에는 은은한 회색 점이 표시됩니다. 마젠타는 피부톤·녹색·청색이 지배적인 자연 영상 배경에서 두드러지므로, 약한 눈의 초점을 끌어당기고 뇌가 두 신호를 하나의 입체 상으로 병합하도록 유도합니다. 웨지 차단 (Wedge Occlusion) : 양쪽 시야에 검은 쐐기 형태를 도입해 각 눈이 장면의 서로 다른 부분만 보게 함으로써 양안 경쟁(binocular rivalry)을 줄입니다. 여기서 흥미로운 엔지니어링 포인트는 이 모든 필터가 스테레오 렌더링 파이프라인에서 좌·우 아이 버퍼에 각각 다른 파라미터로 적용된다는 점입니다. 즉 '동일한 프레임을 두 번 그리는' 일반적인 VR 렌더링과 달리, 눈마다 다른 후처리(post-processing) 체인을 태웁니다. 이건 프레임당 연산 비용이 늘어나는 트레이드오프를 수반하지만, 두 눈에 서로 다른 자극을 주는 훈련에서는 필수적인 구조입니다. 대신 샤프닝과 외곽선 강조는 '사람 형상'이 검출된 영역에만 선택적으로 적용해 비용을 줄입니다. 전체 화면에 필터를 거는 대신 관심 영역(ROI)만 처리하는 셈입니다. 초기 설정 흐름도 임상적 프리셋을 따릅니다. 실행 시 어느 쪽이 약시안인지(좌/우)를 선택하고 — 잘못 선택하면 우세안을 훈련하게 되므로 이 선택은 매우 중요합니다 — 교정 안경을 쓴 상태에서 정도(Mild·Moderate·Severe) 프리셋을 고르면 Dominant Eye Shader와 Lazy Eye Sharpener의 기본 레벨이 자동으로 조정됩니다. 내장된 LogMAR 시력 확인은 가상 3m 거리에서 표준 Landolt C 시표를 사용해 눈별 최대 30회 시행, 임상적 계단식 알고리즘으로 logMAR 시력을 표시하고 검출된 정도에 맞춰 훈련 프로필을 자동 갱신할 수 있습니다. 이 '정도 프리셋'이 실무적으로 왜 중요한지 짚어둘 만합니다. 시각 훈련에서 가장 흔한 실패 모드는 강도가 너무 세서 사용자가 며칠 만에 포기하는 것입니다. Mild·Moderate·Severe 프리셋과 Pulse Hz/depth 조절은 강도를 낮게 시작해 올릴 수 있게 해주는 '접근 가능한 기본값'입니다. 좋은 훈련 도구는 최대 강도가 아니라 지속 가능한 기본값을 제공해야 합니다. 콘텐츠 계층과 훈련 계층의 분리 엔지니어링 관점에서 흥미로운 지점은 Amblyotube가 콘텐츠를 새로 만들지 않는다는 사실입니다. 좋아하는 YouTube 스타일 영상을 그대로 재생하면, 렌더링 계층 위에서 훈련 필터가 실시간으로 얹힙니다. 기본 가상 공간 외에 Room View(AR 패스스루 모드)로 사용자의 실제 방 위에 오버레이해 훈련할 수도 있고, 통합 YouTube 검색과 오프라인 카탈로그(어린이용 영상 포함)도 제공됩니다. 컨트롤 패널은 VR 내에서 크기 조절과 이동이 가능하며 Meta Quest 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 모두 지원합니다. 즉 사용자가 '매일 켤 이유'를 콘텐츠 선택으로 확보하고, 훈련 로직은 그 위에서 독립적으로 동작합니다. 이 분리는 두 가지 이점을 만듭니다. 첫째, 콘텐츠를 새로 만들 필요가 없으므로 사용자가 이미 좋아하는 영상을 그대로 씁니다. 둘째, 훈련 로직이 특정 콘텐츠에 묶이지 않으므로 이식성이 높습니다. 접착식 패치나 적청(anaglyph) 안경이 필요 없다는 점도 이 구조의 부산물입니다. 적청 안경이 장면 전체의 색을 왜곡하는 것과 달리, 이 방식은 자연스러운 색을 유지합니다. 정리: 도구가 일상이 될수록 중요해지는 것 Quest 2 세대의 종료는 VR이 '실험 단계'를 지나 '일상 도구'로 자리 잡았다는 신호이기도 합니다. 도구가 일상이 될수록, 사용자가 자기 훈련을 자기 조건에 맞춰 통제할 수 있는지가 중요해집니다. 하드웨어 세대는 대략 4~6년 주기로 교체되지만, 습관은 그보다 오래갑니다. 그 관점에서 Amblyotube는 특정 세대의 하드웨어가 아니라, 매일 이어지는 루틴에 초점을 맞춥니다. 권장 사용량은 하루 30~40분(세션당 최대 1시간), 만 13세 이상 권장입니다. 중요한 안내 : Amblyotube는 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 위한 보조적 시각 훈련 도구이며, 진단·치료·완치 수단이 아닙니다. 시각 관련 증상이 있다면 의료 전문가와 상담하시기 바랍니다. Meta Quest 앱스토어에서 확인하세요: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

여기서 흥미로운 엔지니어링 포인트는 이 모든 필터가 스테레오 렌더링 파이프라인에서 좌·우 아이 버퍼에 각각 다른 파라미터로 적용된다는 점입니다. 즉 '동일한 프레임을 두 번 그리는' 일반적인 VR 렌더링과 달리, 눈마다 다른 후처리(post-processing) 체인을 태웁니다. 이건 프레임당 연산 비용이 늘어나는 트레이드오프를 수반하지만, 두 눈에 서로 다른 자극을 주는 훈련에서는 필수적인 구조입니다. 대신 샤프닝과 외곽선 강조는 '사람 형상'이 검출된 영역에만 선택적으로 적용해 비용을 줄입니다. 전체 화면에 필터를 거는 대신 관심 영역(ROI)만 처리하는 셈입니다.

초기 설정 흐름도 임상적 프리셋을 따릅니다. 실행 시 어느 쪽이 약시안인지(좌/우)를 선택하고 — 잘못 선택하면 우세안을 훈련하게 되므로 이 선택은 매우 중요합니다 — 교정 안경을 쓴 상태에서 정도(Mild·Moderate·Severe) 프리셋을 고르면 Dominant Eye Shader와 Lazy Eye Sharpener의 기본 레벨이 자동으로 조정됩니다. 내장된 LogMAR 시력 확인은 가상 3m 거리에서 표준 Landolt C 시표를 사용해 눈별 최대 30회 시행, 임상적 계단식 알고리즘으로 logMAR 시력을 표시하고 검출된 정도에 맞춰 훈련 프로필을 자동 갱신할 수 있습니다.

이 '정도 프리셋'이 실무적으로 왜 중요한지 짚어둘 만합니다. 시각 훈련에서 가장 흔한 실패 모드는 강도가 너무 세서 사용자가 며칠 만에 포기하는 것입니다. Mild·Moderate·Severe 프리셋과 Pulse Hz/depth 조절은 강도를 낮게 시작해 올릴 수 있게 해주는 '접근 가능한 기본값'입니다. 좋은 훈련 도구는 최대 강도가 아니라 지속 가능한 기본값을 제공해야 합니다.

콘텐츠 계층과 훈련 계층의 분리

엔지니어링 관점에서 흥미로운 지점은 Amblyotube가 콘텐츠를 새로 만들지 않는다는 사실입니다. 좋아하는 YouTube 스타일 영상을 그대로 재생하면, 렌더링 계층 위에서 훈련 필터가 실시간으로 얹힙니다. 기본 가상 공간 외에 Room View(AR 패스스루 모드)로 사용자의 실제 방 위에 오버레이해 훈련할 수도 있고, 통합 YouTube 검색과 오프라인 카탈로그(어린이용 영상 포함)도 제공됩니다. 컨트롤 패널은 VR 내에서 크기 조절과 이동이 가능하며 Meta Quest 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 모두 지원합니다.

즉 사용자가 '매일 켤 이유'를 콘텐츠 선택으로 확보하고, 훈련 로직은 그 위에서 독립적으로 동작합니다. 이 분리는 두 가지 이점을 만듭니다. 첫째, 콘텐츠를 새로 만들 필요가 없으므로 사용자가 이미 좋아하는 영상을 그대로 씁니다. 둘째, 훈련 로직이 특정 콘텐츠에 묶이지 않으므로 이식성이 높습니다. 접착식 패치나 적청(anaglyph) 안경이 필요 없다는 점도 이 구조의 부산물입니다. 적청 안경이 장면 전체의 색을 왜곡하는 것과 달리, 이 방식은 자연스러운 색을 유지합니다.

정리: 도구가 일상이 될수록 중요해지는 것

Quest 2 세대의 종료는 VR이 '실험 단계'를 지나 '일상 도구'로 자리 잡았다는 신호이기도 합니다. 도구가 일상이 될수록, 사용자가 자기 훈련을 자기 조건에 맞춰 통제할 수 있는지가 중요해집니다. 하드웨어 세대는 대략 4~6년 주기로 교체되지만, 습관은 그보다 오래갑니다. 그 관점에서 Amblyotube는 특정 세대의 하드웨어가 아니라, 매일 이어지는 루틴에 초점을 맞춥니다. 권장 사용량은 하루 30~40분(세션당 최대 1시간), 만 13세 이상 권장입니다.

중요한 안내: Amblyotube는 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 위한 보조적 시각 훈련 도구이며, 진단·치료·완치 수단이 아닙니다. 시각 관련 증상이 있다면 의료 전문가와 상담하시기 바랍니다.

Meta Quest 앱스토어에서 확인하세요: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

items.title: I built a spending guard for AI agents that asks my phone before they pay
items.summary: I've been letting AI agents do more on their own, and at some point I realized that if one decided to buy something or upgrade a plan, nothing would stop it. So I built Saifuban ("wallet keeper" in Japanese). https://ut181749ut.github.io/saifuban/ What it does Before spending money, the agent asks Saifuban whether the payment is OK. Saifuban answers using rules you set: Small amounts under your threshold are approved right away. Anything larger sends a push notification to your phone. You tap Approve or Reject. Payments over the daily budget or the per-payment limit are refused, as are merchants you haven't allowed. A kill switch stops everything at once. Rules are per agent, so a research agent can have $5/day while a coding agent gets more. Saifuban never handles card details or moves money. It only decides whether a payment is allowed. How you connect it It's a remote MCP server, so any client that supports remote MCP can use it with one URL: Claude (custom connector), ChatGPT (developer mode), Cursor, VS Code and so on. Open the site, pick a budget, and paste the URL it gives you. Then ask your agent "check my remaining budget with Saifuban" to confirm it's connected. The agent sees three tools: request_payment : ask whether a payment (merchant, amount, currency, reason) is allowed. It waits up to 45 seconds for you to approve on your phone. check_payment_status : check a pending request later. get_budget : how much is left today. Amounts can be in yen or dollars, and the UI has an English mode. Two things I had to get right Pending requests count against the budget. If they didn't, an agent could fire off ten pending requests, and approving them all would blow straight past the daily limit. So a pending request reserves its amount until it's decided or expires (24 hours). Asking is voluntary. Someone on Reddit pointed out that a prompt-injected agent could simply skip the check. That's true. So every approved request now returns a single-use payment_token that is scoped to the approved merchant and amount, expires in 24 hours, and dies if the agent is stopped. Whatever actually moves the money calls /redeem before paying: curl -X POST https://zrphnuvrsldcycxtdftv.supabase.co/functions/v1/saifuban/redeem \ -H "content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"token":"sbt_...","merchant":"OpenAI","amount":12.5,"currency":"USD"}' A second redeem returns already_used , a different merchant returns merchant_mismatch , and a bigger amount returns amount_exceeds_approval . To be clear, this only becomes hard enforcement when the payment side checks the token. Today that means your own payment code, not third-party checkout. API spend is the one place it's already enforced: if you store your OpenAI, Anthropic or OpenRouter key in Saifuban, the agent only ever gets a proxy key, and requests stop when the budget runs out. Stack Supabase Edge Functions and Postgres. All the rules are checked inside one database function, with a row lock per agent so concurrent requests can't race the budget. The site is a plain-JS PWA on GitHub Pages, and notifications use Web Push with approve/reject buttons right in the notification. Try it It's free and early. I'd love to hear what limits would make you comfortable letting an agent spend, and whether you'd verify tokens on the merchant side. Site: https://ut181749ut.github.io/saifuban/ Repo and issues: https://github.com/ut181749ut/saifuban

https://ut181749ut.github.io/saifuban/

What it does

Before spending money, the agent asks Saifuban whether the payment is OK. Saifuban answers using rules you set:

  • Small amounts under your threshold are approved right away.
  • Anything larger sends a push notification to your phone. You tap Approve or Reject.
  • Payments over the daily budget or the per-payment limit are refused, as are merchants you haven't allowed.
  • A kill switch stops everything at once.

Rules are per agent, so a research agent can have $5/day while a coding agent gets more. Saifuban never handles card details or moves money. It only decides whether a payment is allowed.

How you connect it

It's a remote MCP server, so any client that supports remote MCP can use it with one URL: Claude (custom connector), ChatGPT (developer mode), Cursor, VS Code and so on. Open the site, pick a budget, and paste the URL it gives you. Then ask your agent "check my remaining budget with Saifuban" to confirm it's connected.

The agent sees three tools:

  • request_payment: ask whether a payment (merchant, amount, currency, reason) is allowed. It waits up to 45 seconds for you to approve on your phone.
  • check_payment_status: check a pending request later.
  • get_budget: how much is left today.

Amounts can be in yen or dollars, and the UI has an English mode.

Two things I had to get right

Pending requests count against the budget. If they didn't, an agent could fire off ten pending requests, and approving them all would blow straight past the daily limit. So a pending request reserves its amount until it's decided or expires (24 hours).

Asking is voluntary. Someone on Reddit pointed out that a prompt-injected agent could simply skip the check. That's true. So every approved request now returns a single-use payment_token that is scoped to the approved merchant and amount, expires in 24 hours, and dies if the agent is stopped. Whatever actually moves the money calls /redeem before paying:

curl -X POST https://zrphnuvrsldcycxtdftv.supabase.co/functions/v1/saifuban/redeem \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"token":"sbt_...","merchant":"OpenAI","amount":12.5,"currency":"USD"}'

A second redeem returns already_used, a different merchant returns merchant_mismatch, and a bigger amount returns amount_exceeds_approval. To be clear, this only becomes hard enforcement when the payment side checks the token. Today that means your own payment code, not third-party checkout.

API spend is the one place it's already enforced: if you store your OpenAI, Anthropic or OpenRouter key in Saifuban, the agent only ever gets a proxy key, and requests stop when the budget runs out.

Stack

Supabase Edge Functions and Postgres. All the rules are checked inside one database function, with a row lock per agent so concurrent requests can't race the budget. The site is a plain-JS PWA on GitHub Pages, and notifications use Web Push with approve/reject buttons right in the notification.

Try it

It's free and early. I'd love to hear what limits would make you comfortable letting an agent spend, and whether you'd verify tokens on the merchant side.

  • Repo and issues: https://github.com/ut181749ut/saifuban

items.title: Vary Is Not a Privacy Boundary for Authenticated Responses
items.summary: Vary Is Not a Privacy Boundary for Authenticated Responses An HTTP cache can save bandwidth and reduce latency, but it also makes decisions about which request may reuse a stored response. The Vary response header tells caches which request header fields contributed to the response. RFC 9111 requires a cache to avoid reusing a stored response unless the nominated header fields match the original request, or the cache revalidates the response. That is a correctness rule for content negotiation. It is not a promise that a shared cache will protect private data. A common mistake is to vary on Accept-Encoding or User-Agent while forgetting the cookie or authorization context that produced the body. If a response contains a personalized account panel and the cache key does not include the relevant identity, a second request can receive the first user's body. Adding Vary: Cookie can reduce the risk in some deployments, but it is a blunt instrument. Cookie values change frequently, can contain sensitive data, and may not be normalized consistently across cache nodes. RFC 9111 also discusses responses to requests containing Authorization . A shared cache generally cannot reuse that response unless a response directive permits it and the reuse rules are satisfied. Teams should not depend on a proxy to infer privacy from an authentication header. Mark sensitive responses with Cache-Control: private or another policy that matches the data. Use no-store when retaining the response would create a recovery or device-storage problem, while recognizing that it may disable useful browser history behavior. Cache-key design should be explicit. List the headers that affect the response, normalize their values, and test the exact variants that production will send. Decide whether the cache is browser-local, CDN-shared, or application-level. A CDN may have its own key configuration that ignores or rewrites an origin's Vary header. The security review should inspect both the origin response and the edge configuration. A small test can expose a large problem. Create two accounts with different display names. Request the same URL through the proxy with each account. Confirm that the response body, status, and cache headers differ as expected. Repeat with the first request missing a cookie, a malformed cookie, and an expired session. Inspect the cache's hit or miss reason. If the edge reports a hit for a response that should be private, treat it as a data exposure until proven otherwise. Content negotiation is not the only source of variants. Localization, feature flags, tenant routing, device class, and experiments can all change a response. Add a variation only after deciding what the response depends on and how the cache will isolate it. A custom header used for a private experiment should not become a global cache key unless every proxy understands it. A header that is absent in some requests can create a shared fallback that leaks the first variant. For incident response, cache poisoning and cache leakage need different questions. Cache poisoning asks who could influence the stored response. Cache leakage asks who could read it. Both require the cache key and the response policy. Preserve proxy logs and the origin's Vary and Cache-Control headers. Do not clear a shared cache without first collecting evidence about which user or tenant received the response. Vary is useful and necessary when the origin truly negotiates content. It is not a substitute for private caching rules. A safe design names the response's sensitivity, chooses a cache scope, creates a key that covers every relevant input, and verifies the behavior through the actual edge. The cache should be fast because the team knows what may be reused, not because nobody checked. References RFC 9111: HTTP Caching RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics MDN: Cache-Control header

items.title: PR Pilot: Putting Multi-Agent AI Code Reviewers Inside Discord
items.summary: This is a submission for the MLH x DEV Writing Challenge What I Built Every developer knows the dread of the Pull Request bottleneck : you push a feature, open a PR, and... silence. Days pass. Context is lost. Reviewers get dragged away by meetings, while authors juggle stale branches. Meanwhile, your team chat (Discord/Slack) is buzzing with activity, completely disconnected from what’s happening on GitHub. To bridge this divide, I built PR Pilot : an automated, dual-agent AI code review system that lives directly inside your team's Discord #pr-reviews channel. Instead of a noisy bot that just dumps notifications, PR Pilot acts like two junior-to-senior pair programmers sitting in the room: @pr-reviewer (The Strategic Reviewer) : Ingests the GitHub diff upon PR creation. Summarizes the "why" and "what" in 2–3 concise sentences. Assesses a risk tier ( LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH ) targeting security, auth, migrations, and breaking changes. Prompts the author with 2–3 pointed questions about edge cases and maintainability. Listens for team instructions: typing approve or request changes will execute the actual GitHub API review directly from Discord! @pr-standards (The Automated Gatekeeper) : Triggered automatically by @pr-reviewer . Runs an objective 6-point checklist: ✅ Conventional Commit title ( feat: , fix: , etc.) ✅ Non-empty description explaining the intent ⚠️ Test coverage check (flags if source changed without tests) ✅ Unlinked TODO / FIXME detection (must cite issue numbers) ✅ Documentation updates for public APIs / config ✅ PR diff size check (< 400 lines) How It Works ┌──────────────┐ GitHub Webhook ┌─────────────────┐ SSE / Room Event ┌──────────────────┐ │ GitHub │ ─────────────────► │ PR Pilot │ ───────────────────► │ Switch Server │ │ (PR event) │ │ Webhook Receiver│ │ (Local / Docker) │ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ │ Discord Bridge ┌────────▼─────────┐ │ Discord │ │ #pr-reviews │ │ │ │ @pr-reviewer │ │ @pr-standards │ │ 👤 Team Humans │ └──────────────────┘ │ GitHub API Execution (Approve / Block) A developer opens a PR on GitHub. A GitHub webhook hits the PR Pilot FastAPI service. The event routes to the Discord room through Switch . @pr-reviewer reads the diff, writes a review, and tags @pr-standards . @pr-standards posts its pass/warn/fail scorecard. Teammates can ask questions in the thread, discuss with the AI, and type approve to officially approve the PR on GitHub without ever leaving Discord. Demo 📦 GitHub Repository : github.com/jaysid97/pr-pilot 📹 Demo Walkthrough Video : [Insert your demo video link or walkthrough here] Live Walkthrough in Discord Here is what the interaction looks like when a developer opens a pull request: PR Opened: feat: add JWT authentication logic (#42) @pr-reviewer : 🔍 Summary : Implements JWT verification middleware and token renewal endpoints. ⚠️ Risk Level : HIGH — modifies core authentication logic and security headers. ❓ Questions for @author : Have we accounted for token replay prevention during silent refresh? Is the secret rotation strategy compatible with multi-instance clustering? @pr-standards please run your checklist on this PR: https://github.com/demo/repo/pull/42 @pr-standards : 📋 Standards Check for PR #42 : ✅ Conventional commit title ✅ Description present ⚠️ No test files updated ( tests/test_auth.py missing) ✅ No unlinked TODOs ✅ PR size: 142 lines (healthy) Overall : PASS with 1 warning. Developer : "Does this handle token refresh edge cases?" @pr-reviewer : "Yes, in auth_service.py:84 , expired tokens return 401 TOKEN_EXPIRED , but network retry backoff should still be handled by the client." Developer : "approve" @pr-reviewer : "✅ Approved on GitHub on behalf of @developer." Partner Technologies 1. Switch Switch served as the foundational infrastructure for PR Pilot. Rather than building custom Discord bot handlers, websocket daemons, and session trackers from scratch: Declarative Room Templates : With pr-pilot.template.yaml , the entire multi-agent environment (agent identities, instruction prompts, communication policies, and channel bindings) is spin-up ready in a single click via Switch Console. Agent Communication Protocol : @pr-reviewer and @pr-standards consume room events via Server-Sent Events (SSE) and post through HTTP back to Switch. Discord Bridge : Switch translates bidirectional messages between Discord's API and the agents seamlessly, allowing agents to react to human input in natural conversational threads. 2. Antigravity & Agent Runtimes I leveraged Antigravity to formulate the agent personalities, system prompts, and strict guardrails. The dual-agent separation prevents prompt bloat: @pr-reviewer specializes in qualitative reasoning, code comprehension, and API execution, while @pr-standards operates as a deterministic, objective checklist engine. 3. FastAPI & Docker The webhook receiver was built with FastAPI, containerized using Docker Compose, and securely exposed via tunnels to handle GitHub payload verification ( HMAC-SHA256 ) and dispatch events to the Switch network with sub-second latency. Hackathon Experience Building PR Pilot during the hackathon was an absolute blast. Hackathons are famous for high adrenaline and tight timelines, but the biggest revelation for me was how natural multi-agent architectures feel when anchored inside a team chat application. Instead of isolating AI into web dashboards or CLI tools that people forget to check, putting them where developers already hang out (Discord) transforms AI from a passive utility into an active pair-programming teammate. The most memorable moment was testing the full loop for the first time: pushing a mock breaking commit, watching Discord light up 3 seconds later with a targeted warning from @pr-reviewer , discussing it in the channel, and seeing the PR status tick green on GitHub just by typing "approve" in chat. What's Next for PR Pilot Support for GitLab and Bitbucket webhooks. Inline PR code comment suggestions directly generated from Discord threads. Custom organization rulebooks that let teams define their own @pr-standards checklists via simple YAML files. Check out the repository on GitHub and feel free to try running the Switch template in your own server! Let me know in the comments how your team manages pull request reviews.

    • Summarizes the "why" and "what" in 2–3 concise sentences.
    • Assesses a risk tier (LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH) targeting security, auth, migrations, and breaking changes.
    • Prompts the author with 2–3 pointed questions about edge cases and maintainability.
    • Listens for team instructions: typing approve or request changes will execute the actual GitHub API review directly from Discord!

  2. @pr-standards (The Automated Gatekeeper):

    • Triggered automatically by @pr-reviewer.
    • Runs an objective 6-point checklist:
      • ✅ Conventional Commit title (feat:, fix:, etc.)
      • ✅ Non-empty description explaining the intent
      • ⚠️ Test coverage check (flags if source changed without tests)
      • ✅ Unlinked TODO / FIXME detection (must cite issue numbers)
      • ✅ Documentation updates for public APIs / config
      • ✅ PR diff size check (< 400 lines)

└──────────────┘                    └─────────────────┘                      └────────┬─────────┘
                                                                                      │ Discord Bridge
                                                                             ┌────────▼─────────┐
                                                                             │     Discord      │
                                                                             │   #pr-reviews    │
                                                                             │                  │

                                                                             │  @pr-standards   │

  1. A developer opens a PR on GitHub.
  2. A GitHub webhook hits the PR Pilot FastAPI service.
  3. The event routes to the Discord room through Switch.
  4. @pr-reviewer reads the diff, writes a review, and tags @pr-standards.
  5. @pr-standards posts its pass/warn/fail scorecard.
  6. Teammates can ask questions in the thread, discuss with the AI, and type approve to officially approve the PR on GitHub without ever leaving Discord.
Demo

  • 📹 Demo Walkthrough Video: [Insert your demo video link or walkthrough here]
Live Walkthrough in Discord

Here is what the interaction looks like when a developer opens a pull request:

PR Opened: feat: add JWT authentication logic (#42)

@pr-reviewer:

🔍 Summary: Implements JWT verification middleware and token renewal endpoints.
⚠️ Risk Level: HIGH — modifies core authentication logic and security headers.
❓ Questions for @author:

  1. Have we accounted for token replay prevention during silent refresh?
  2. Is the secret rotation strategy compatible with multi-instance clustering?

@pr-standards please run your checklist on this PR: https://github.com/demo/repo/pull/42

@pr-standards:

📋 Standards Check for PR #42:

  • ✅ Conventional commit title
  • ✅ Description present
  • ⚠️ No test files updated (tests/test_auth.py missing)
  • ✅ No unlinked TODOs
  • ✅ PR size: 142 lines (healthy)

Overall: PASS with 1 warning.

Developer: "Does this handle token refresh edge cases?"

@pr-reviewer: "Yes, in auth_service.py:84, expired tokens return 401 TOKEN_EXPIRED, but network retry backoff should still be handled by the client."

Developer: "approve"

@pr-reviewer: "✅ Approved on GitHub on behalf of @developer."

Partner Technologies 1. Switch

Switch served as the foundational infrastructure for PR Pilot. Rather than building custom Discord bot handlers, websocket daemons, and session trackers from scratch:

  • Declarative Room Templates: With pr-pilot.template.yaml, the entire multi-agent environment (agent identities, instruction prompts, communication policies, and channel bindings) is spin-up ready in a single click via Switch Console.
  • Agent Communication Protocol: @pr-reviewer and @pr-standards consume room events via Server-Sent Events (SSE) and post through HTTP back to Switch.
  • Discord Bridge: Switch translates bidirectional messages between Discord's API and the agents seamlessly, allowing agents to react to human input in natural conversational threads.
2. Antigravity & Agent Runtimes

I leveraged Antigravity to formulate the agent personalities, system prompts, and strict guardrails. The dual-agent separation prevents prompt bloat: @pr-reviewer specializes in qualitative reasoning, code comprehension, and API execution, while @pr-standards operates as a deterministic, objective checklist engine.

3. FastAPI & Docker

The webhook receiver was built with FastAPI, containerized using Docker Compose, and securely exposed via tunnels to handle GitHub payload verification (HMAC-SHA256) and dispatch events to the Switch network with sub-second latency.

Hackathon Experience

Building PR Pilot during the hackathon was an absolute blast.

Hackathons are famous for high adrenaline and tight timelines, but the biggest revelation for me was how natural multi-agent architectures feel when anchored inside a team chat application. Instead of isolating AI into web dashboards or CLI tools that people forget to check, putting them where developers already hang out (Discord) transforms AI from a passive utility into an active pair-programming teammate.

The most memorable moment was testing the full loop for the first time: pushing a mock breaking commit, watching Discord light up 3 seconds later with a targeted warning from @pr-reviewer, discussing it in the channel, and seeing the PR status tick green on GitHub just by typing "approve" in chat.

What's Next for PR Pilot
  • Support for GitLab and Bitbucket webhooks.
  • Inline PR code comment suggestions directly generated from Discord threads.
  • Custom organization rulebooks that let teams define their own @pr-standards checklists via simple YAML files.

Check out the repository on GitHub and feel free to try running the Switch template in your own server! Let me know in the comments how your team manages pull request reviews.

items.summary: Understand the five-hour and weekly limits, check when they reset, and make your Claude Code usage go further. Illustration generated with AI. You are in the middle of a task when Claude Code stops because you have reached a usage limit. You start a new session, hoping to continue, but your plan allowance is already exhausted. A new conversation does not refill it. So you check /usage, but now you have another question: which number explains the problem, and what can you actually do about it? A full context window, a five-hour limit, and a weekly limit can all interrupt your workflow. They do not mean the same thing, and the wrong response can leave you right where you started. Even the recommendations can be easy to misread. Suppose /usage shows “25%” beside a suggestion. That does not mean following it will save you 25% of your allowance. It tells you how much recent usage the recommendation applies to. Let’s work out which limit you have hit, when it resets, and how to test changes that might help your Claude Code usage last longer. The scenario and number are illustrative, not results from a test. Documentation checked November 7, 2026. Plan rules, commands, and displays can change; check the linked Anthropic documentation and your account for current details. If you need a next step now, start with the message or number you see: Context window nearly full: use /context to inspect it and consider /compact, or start a fresh session for unrelated work. Save any details you still need first. Plan usage limit reached: check /usage or Settings > Usage for the affected limit and its reset time. Depending on your account, you may also have a separate reset or a paid option available. A dollar figure in /usage: check how you authenticated and your provider’s actual billing. The session figure is an estimate, not necessarily a charge. Claude Code usage limits vs. context window: which one did you hit? Suppose you have been working on a bug for hours. Claude says the conversation is approaching its context limit, but your plan still has capacity. The immediate problem is the conversation’s size, not an exhausted weekly allowance. Compacting the conversation or starting a fresh session for unrelated work can help make room. Now change the example: the weekly plan limit is exhausted, but the conversation itself isn’t full. Starting a fresh session will not refill that allowance. Check which limit was reached and when it resets in /usage or your account’s usage settings. If it’s the shorter session window, the relevant reset may arrive sooner than the weekly reset. If it’s the weekly window, check that reset instead. Depending on your account and settings, you may need to wait, change plans, or consider an available paid option. Switching models does not restore an exhausted shared allowance. The distinction is easier to remember if you think of the context window as a working desk: it holds the instructions, messages, files, and tool results used in a conversation. Your plan allowance measures usage over time across supported Claude products. API billing is a separate question again: what is charged for API use? Author-created conceptual diagram based on Anthropic’s usage guidance and cost documentation . When do the five-hour and weekly limits reset? For individual Pro and Max plans, Anthropic describes both a five-hour session limit and a weekly limit. The five-hour window starts with your first message and resets five hours later. The weekly limit resets at a fixed time assigned to your account. Verified Ultra accounts have a weekly limit without the five-hour limit; other conditions can apply. Check your own reset times under Settings > Usage . Usage depends on factors including the model, effort, conversation length, and features used. See Anthropic’s explanation of usage and length limits for your plan’s current rules. Some eligible accounts occasionally receive a separate limit reset that can restore a specified five-hour or weekly allowance early. If one is available, Anthropic says it appears under Settings > Usage on the web or Claude Desktop; check the offer and any expiry before using it. It does not change the normal weekly reset time or refund charges. The reset option is not currently available inside Claude Code, though a reset used in Claude also affects the shared Claude Code allowance. See Anthropic’s limit reset guide for details and eligibility. How to check Claude Code usage with /usage Suppose you open /usage after seeing that your weekly allowance is running low. On supported subscription plans, the display can include plan usage bars, activity statistics, an attribution breakdown, and recommendations. The available details can depend on your plan and Claude Code version. Here is the important boundary: the plan bars represent the account allowance, while the detailed attribution and recommendations are approximate and based on this machine’s local session history . Activity on another computer or on claude.ai does not appear in that local breakdown, even though Claude and Claude Code can share the allowance. If the breakdown does not explain the full account total, that gap is not necessarily an error. Suppose one recommendation has “25%” next to it. It means the recommendation applies to roughly a quarter of the recent usage covered by the analysis. It does not mean implementing it will save 25%. A request may also be counted in several recommendation rows, so those percentages can add up to more than 100%. Attribution shares, which associate usage with features such as subagents or individual MCP servers, answer a different question from recommendation shares. Anthropic’s cost guide explains both. Let’s say the recommendation concerns a large project instruction file. The next move is to inspect that file and remove only instructions that are redundant or irrelevant, while keeping essential project rules. Then compare a repeatable task with the original and revised instructions, keeping its checks the same. Even if the file was involved in 25% of recent local activity, the result of trimming it remains an open question. We’ll make that comparison more concrete below. Are you looking at a subscription limit or an API bill? The same /usage display can show a session cost in dollars, calculated locally from token counts using API list prices or configured organizational rates. For a subscriber, that figure is not automatically a charge on a card. For API users, it is still an estimate rather than an invoice. Check actual provider billing separately, especially if additional paid usage is enabled. Claude Code’s cost guide describes the distinction. Authentication matters too. Anthropic warns that an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in your environment can cause Claude Code to use the API instead of your subscription, with API charges. Check your account and billing arrangement before assuming which one is active. Anthropic’s plan guide explains the distinction. A subscription user may want an allowance to last until its reset. An API user may be managing a bill. A dollar estimate and a percentage of a plan are different measurements, even when the same task produces both. How to reduce usage: start with context Long conversations carry useful history: failed attempts, test output, and decisions can all help with a difficult bug. Trouble starts when unrelated work carries that history along for no reason. Suppose you finish debugging authentication and then investigate an unrelated build configuration. /clear starts a new session with a cleaner conversation. First, save the details you still need somewhere appropriate for the project. A new session may need to rediscover context, so clearing repeatedly in the middle of one connected task can be counterproductive. For a long task that is still connected, /compact summarizes the conversation. You can ask it to preserve the current failure, decisions, and test results. A summary is not a perfect copy; check it when exact context matters. Use /context to inspect what occupies the current window. It can reveal instructions or tools you do not need, but it does not tell you that removing an item will save a precise share of your weekly allowance. Clearing or compacting does not reset that allowance either. Choose the right model and effort level A difficult production bug, a small naming change, and a documentation lookup put different demands on a model. Anthropic’s Claude Code guidance describes using a more capable model for harder reasoning and a smaller one for routine work. You can inspect models available to your account and switch with /model. Where supported, a lower effort setting is another option for less demanding work. This is not a rule to use the smallest model everywhere. A lighter first attempt that misses an important constraint and needs several rounds of repair may cost more work overall. Consider the full task: implementation, verification, and correction. Keep the acceptance checks the same when comparing approaches. Account for subagents and MCP tools A subagent can handle a noisy search or a long investigation and return a concise summary, leaving the main conversation easier to navigate. But the subagent makes its own requests, and those requests count toward usage. Several agents working in parallel can each need context and independently inspect files or call tools. Use a subagent when a bounded, independent task benefits from delegation. Moving work away from the main conversation does not make it free. For a small lookup, doing it directly may be enough. For a separate review or investigation, the additional work may be worthwhile. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, a way to connect Claude to outside tools and data sources, such as a project tracker. Those connections and their tool results can add context and work. Claude Code’s documentation says tool definitions are deferred by default, so not every tool description is loaded upfront; /context helps show what is present, while /mcp lets you inspect configured servers. Disable an unneeded server only if it is safe to do so. An essential tool can be worth its cost. Try a small comparison before changing your workflow Return to the hypothetical instruction-file recommendation. Here is one way to investigate it without pretending the recommendation itself predicts a saving: Choose a repeatable task. For example, take the same small bug fix from the same starting commit in two separate clean copies of a project. Write down the prompt and the tests and review criteria that an acceptable patch must pass. Change one thing. Use the original instruction file for one version and a carefully trimmed file for the other. Keep the model, effort setting, prompt, tools, starting code, and acceptance checks the same. Run each in a fresh session and record the setup. Record before and after. Note the relevant plan bars and reset times, and record the session token information and estimated cost shown in /usage where available. Save the numbers before clearing a session. Also record test results, time, and any human correction or follow-up needed. API users should check provider usage and billing records for actual charges. Compare completed outcomes. A smaller number is not a win if the patch fails the checks or needs significant rework. Repeat the comparison across several runs when practical, and look at variation rather than declaring a saving from one attempt. This is an experiment you can run, not a benchmark I performed. Shared Claude activity can move plan bars during the comparison; the local attribution is incomplete; caching and ordinary run-to-run variation can affect the result. Plan bars may be too coarse to isolate a small task at all. If the available data cannot distinguish the approaches, the honest result is that you do not know yet. Start by identifying the limit, then check the number that belongs to it. When you change your workflow, judge the finished result as well as the meter. The available data can guide that decision, even when it cannot account for every request or promise a specific saving. items.title: The Mathematics Behind Artificial Intelligence: How Linear Algebra Makes Machines Learn
items.summary: Cover Image Behind every intelligent system, there is a language of numbers, vectors and metrices. From identifying human language to generating images and making predictions, Artificial Intelligence relies heavily on mathematical structures that allow systems to represent, process and learn from information. Among the many branches of Mathematics, Linear Algebra stands as one of the main fundamental pillars of modern AI . Yet its role extends far beyond simply arranging numbers into rows and columns. Vectors represent information, matrices transform data mathematical operations enable neural networks to learn complex patterns hidden within large datasets. In this article, we will explore how Linear Algebra works behind the surface of AI. Why does AI need Linear Algebra? In Artificial Intelligent systems, at its core, the AI model recieves information, represents it in a mathematical form, processes those information by using a huge amount of mathematical calculations and produces output. The input can be a text, image, video or any other input type. But, AI models, even computers cannot identify or understand those inputs and process them as humans do. They use a mathematical representation to store and process those. This is where Linear Algebra becomes important. It provides an efficient way to store data using matrices and vectors. Also, it provides an efficient way to perform the mathematical operations required to transform those data into a meaningful output. As AI models become more complex and datasets grow larger, these representations allow computations to be effective and organized. With billions of Mathematical operations involving matrices and vectors, Modern AI systems appear to be intelligent. From Real-World information to Mathematical Vectors Imagine providing a picture of a cat to the AI System. To a human, with a single glance, the information about the picture such as, shape of the ears, color of the furs and the color, position of eyes can be observed. But, for a computer, a picture is a collection of a numerical pixel values. Each pixel contains a numerical value about its color and intensity. These values can be organized into mathematical structures that AI model can process. This is where Vectors are used. What is a vector? In Linear Algebra, a vector is an ordered collection of numbers that can represent a point in a mathematical space or encode a set of features describing an object. eg :- A simplified representation of an image might be expressed as, X = [0.2, 0.8, 0.5, 0.1] where each number represents a particular pixel value or a feature. Although this example contains only four values, real images may contain thousands or millions of numerical values. Similarly, an AI model can represent person’s characteristics, a piece of text or a collection of measurements as a vector. When these information are converted into vectors, AI model can perform calculations, identify relationships and learn patterns from the data. Vectors are the fundamental component between the complex real — world information and the mathematical computations that make AI possible . Image to Vector Matrices While vectors provide a way to represent single pieces of information, matrices allow to organize and store large collections of numerical data. A Matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns and it plays an important role in Artificial Intelligence. Consider an image of containing thousands of pixels. items.title: How to Enable Wish-Driven Programming With an Autonomous Multi-Agent Framework
items.summary: Make a wish. Take a nap. Wake up to a built feature. Accept the changes. Wish, sleep, accept, repeat. In three weeks, I shipped an AI-native application to the CEO. Wish-driven programming at a glance. What wish-driven programming is DeepSeek introduced the term wish-driven programming (许愿式编程) on 17 October 2026, as the headline of its model release. DeepSeek did not define this concept, here is my interpretation. In wish-driven programming, the human requests a deliverable, such as a feature, an artifact, or a report, and accepts it when it is done. Agents do everything in between: planning, implementation, testing, reviews. Wish-driven programming is an autopilot mode of working, as opposed to a copilot mode. In copilot mode, the human sits inside the loop, so one person’s attention caps throughput. In autopilot mode, the human sits at the two ends of the loop. It frees the human’s attention and productivity at the cost of controls. The term names an outcome, not a method. It does not say how agents can be trusted to work unattended, and an autopilot without built-in quality assurance is only vibe coding at scale. The question for this post is therefore which framework produces the outcome reliably, and what it gains. Proof first Before I show you the framework itself, I want to show what it delivered. Recently, I built an AI-native application for the CEO, solo, in three weeks. A designer gave me the UI design. Agents did everything else. I did not write a single line of code. On the peak day, the agents added 17.6K lines of code. That is about 10 times an average day of a top-10% Cursor developer, or 124 times a median Cursor developer ( Cursor usage data, Spring 2026 ). Figure 1. 3-week building history with the proposed coding framework. Productivity measured in daily line of codes, benchmarking Cursor developers. The framework The framework is a multi-agent framework inspired by Superpowers ’s workstream and Anthropic’s orchestration ( Anthropic, 2026 ), which suggests a strong orchestrator holds the plan and delegates each step to a role subagent that works in its own context. The framework has three components. Agents and subagents do the work. Tools give them their capabilities. Workstreams define repeatable sequences of steps, with quality assurance built in. The framework is not limited to programming: it fits any task that agents can split into steps and verify, such as research. The concepts carry over across platforms, though the configuration files may differ. The design has three benefits. First, the orchestrator’s context stays clean , because subagents return summaries and not their working history. The agent also controls its own handover: it decides what to carry forward, instead of leaving that choice to an automatic compaction. Second, independent tasks run in parallel , each in its own git worktree, which shortens the wall-clock time. Third, the orchestrator matches each task to the right subagent and model , reserving the strongest model for planning and review. I present these as design reasons, not as measured gains over a single agent. Why not a single agent? A single agent can run in autopilot mode, but it risks breaking down on long jobs for two reasons. First, accuracy falls as the context grows: in one 2026 agentic benchmark, three frontier models lost about half to two thirds of their accuracy between 8K and 128K tokens ( LOCA-bench ). Auto-compaction does not fix this and can drop the agent’s instructions, with policy violations rising from 0% to 30% in one 2026 study ( Chen, 2026 ). Second, one agent runs one model for the whole job, which makes it hard to match capability and cost to each task. The orchestrator design answers both: a clean context for the first, a matched model for the second. Agents and subagents The framework has one and only one primary agent, the orchestrator, and multiple subagents. OpenCode, for example, defaults to two primary agents, Build and Plan. I find it unnecessary, because even the Build agent recognizes plan tasks well from built-in workstreams. Other primary agents disrupt the flow. Orchestrator The orchestrator functions as the project lead. It holds the goal and the plan, splits the work into tasks, decides which tasks are independent enough to run in parallel, delegates each task to a subagent, checks and integrates the results, and reports to the human. It does minimal work itself, which keeps its context clean. The orchestrator needs: Model: a strong model like Opus 5.5. Since this is your primary agent, you may switch the model depending on the tasks. Instructions: the R&R boundary of each subagent. Better undefined than duplicated. Tools: discussed in the next section. Subagents Subagents can be defined by role, such as implementer, reviewer and researcher, or by model. Both work, and the choice is a personal preference. The hard requirement is the same either way: each subagent needs a clear R&R boundary that does not overlap with any other, and it is bound to one model-reasoning level, unless the platform supports dynamic orchestration such as Claude’s dynamic workflows. Table 1 shows the roster I used for OpenCode, with R&R boundaries curated from Artificial Analysis . Table 1. My OpenCode subagent roster. This is an example for illustration, not a universal solution. Some best practices in subagent assignment: Implementation: a weaker model, which avoids overthinking. Challenging work such as debugging: a strong model. Repetitive work such as research across sources: multiple cheap models in parallel. Review: a different family than the planner and the implementer. For example, plan with Opus 5.5, implement with Sonnet 5.5, and review with GPT-6.1-sol ( Panickssery et al., 2024 ; Goel et al., 2025 ). Set a step cap for each subagent. Step repetition was among the most frequent failure modes of multi-agent systems ( Cemri et al., 2025 ). Call a reviewer subagent only at major milestones and critical steps. Frequent reviews by a different model family confuse the implementer. I paid my tuition for this lesson. (Optional) Control subagent access to authorization and tools to deterministically enforce R&R boundaries. Tools Tools enable the agents to perform tasks. Types of tools include: Connectors , aka MCP: the toolbox. Skills : the operation manual. Hooks : the safety interlocks. They act on rule-based triggers, independent of the LLM. Plugins : the three tools above, sometimes plus subagents, in a bundle. One may individualize tool access for each agent and subagent for better control and context engineering, at the cost of management complexity. Workstreams The workstreams are what separate this framework from an autopilot without checks, guiding agent-subagent interactions. They may be integrated as a skill for the primary agent to load on demand. Here are three simple, practical examples. Research Figure 2. The research workstream. It uses a fan-out structure to speed up the work. Evaluation Figure 3. The evaluation workstream. It automates test and evaluation processes with an A/B test on a golden dataset and LLM-as-a-judge. Feature development Figure 4. The feature development workstream, inspired by Superpowers. Superpowers is a popular open-source coding agent workstream to start with. It incorporates several valuable development concepts: subagent-driven development (SDD), spec-driven development, test-driven development (TDD), and brainstorming with mock-ups. I updated the Superpowers workstream from a couple of usage frictions to propose this feature development workstream. Key changes are: Invoke the reviewer subagent after each development stage. Superpowers invokes the reviewer after each task. That approach magnifies the model differences, and usually overcomplicates the development. Encourage parallel subagent-driven development. Add the optional research and evaluation workstreams from the previous examples. Limits and what comes next This framework is not a universal solution. A couple of limitations: It is simple, not optimal. I share this framework because it is robust, easy to set up, and easy for beginners to understand. Other advanced frameworks are available, see below. The human is still a limit. Agents cannot replace good taste. Autopilot trades control for attention. Though the framework is autonomous, the human is welcome to engage mid-stream on reviews and approvals for better quality control. Other frameworks to explore: Matt Pocock’s skills (311k): small, composable skills for everyday engineering. ECC (296k): an agent harness with a large catalog of agents, skills, hooks and memory. spec-kit (147k): GitHub’s spec-driven development scaffolding. ruflo (81k): a meta-harness with agent swarms, memory and hooks. oh-my-openagent (71k): a harness that routes each task to a model by role. BMAD-METHOD (55k): an agile method with persona agents. dsh-superagent (16.5k): DeepSeek’s Super Agent, a research prototype of a proactive coding agent. pstack (15k, parent repo): a Cursor-first library of 23 playbooks. Autopilot is not always the right mode. The next article compares autopilot with copilot, the mode where the human works inside the loop. It asks when each mode fits, what each costs in attention and control, and how to move between them during one project. One may individualize tool access for each agent and subagent for better control and context engineering, at the cost of management complexity.

Workstreams

The workstreams are what separate this framework from an autopilot without checks, guiding agent-subagent interactions. They may be integrated as a skill for the primary agent to load on demand. Here are three simple, practical examples.

Research

Figure 2. The research workstream. It uses a fan-out structure to speed up the work.

Evaluation

Figure 3. The evaluation workstream. It automates test and evaluation processes with an A/B test on a golden dataset and LLM-as-a-judge.

Feature development

Figure 4. The feature development workstream, inspired by Superpowers.

Superpowers is a popular open-source coding agent workstream to start with. It incorporates several valuable development concepts: subagent-driven development (SDD), spec-driven development, test-driven development (TDD), and brainstorming with mock-ups.

I updated the Superpowers workstream from a couple of usage frictions to propose this feature development workstream. Key changes are:

  • Invoke the reviewer subagent after each development stage. Superpowers invokes the reviewer after each task. That approach magnifies the model differences, and usually overcomplicates the development.
  • Encourage parallel subagent-driven development.
  • Add the optional research and evaluation workstreams from the previous examples.
Limits and what comes next

This framework is not a universal solution. A couple of limitations:

  • It is simple, not optimal. I share this framework because it is robust, easy to set up, and easy for beginners to understand. Other advanced frameworks are available, see below.
  • The human is still a limit. Agents cannot replace good taste.
  • Autopilot trades control for attention. Though the framework is autonomous, the human is welcome to engage mid-stream on reviews and approvals for better quality control.

Other frameworks to explore:

  • Matt Pocock’s skills (311k): small, composable skills for everyday engineering.
  • ECC (296k): an agent harness with a large catalog of agents, skills, hooks and memory.
  • spec-kit (147k): GitHub’s spec-driven development scaffolding.
  • ruflo (81k): a meta-harness with agent swarms, memory and hooks.
  • oh-my-openagent (71k): a harness that routes each task to a model by role.
  • BMAD-METHOD (55k): an agile method with persona agents.
  • dsh-superagent (16.5k): DeepSeek’s Super Agent, a research prototype of a proactive coding agent.
  • pstack (15k, parent repo): a Cursor-first library of 23 playbooks.

Autopilot is not always the right mode. The next article compares autopilot with copilot, the mode where the human works inside the loop. It asks when each mode fits, what each costs in attention and control, and how to move between them during one project.

In Parquet the saving is smaller, because the readings that report-by-exception drops are exactly the ones that compress best: values that didn’t change, at regular intervals. A good columnar format already removes much of that redundancy on its own. Report-by-exception still matters, mainly for the broker, the network and every consumer that has to process each message.
