One day of a virtual bottling plant, stored eleven different ways. The winner is 51 times smaller than the raw messages, and two of the “optimizations” along the way made things worse.

A pressure sensor reports 800.53 mbar. The number takes six characters, but the message carrying it through the Unified Namespace takes 134 bytes.

That gap is easy to ignore with one sensor. A plant with a few thousand signals publishes millions of such messages a day. Most teams that decide to “just keep the history” start by writing those messages to disk as they arrive. That is a sensible first step, and an expensive one if it becomes the long-term format.

In Part 2 we built a virtual factory: three lines, eight machines, 37 signals, faults, frozen sensors and network outages, all deterministic from a single seed. This post uses one simulated day of that factory to answer a narrow question with real numbers: how much space does this data take, and which storage decisions actually matter?

The setup

The experiment simulates 24 hours of the plant, with seed 42 and report-by-exception enabled. That produces 1,158,046 published readings. The same table is then written in eleven formats:

  • Text formats: JSON lines (one raw MQTT message per line, topic plus payload) and CSV, each with and without gzip.
  • Parquet with different codecs: uncompressed, snappy and zstd.
  • Parquet tuned further: a different sort order, delta-encoded timestamps, byte-stream-split floats, and a different way of storing the delivery time.

Each variant is written three times, and the median write time is reported. For Parquet, the script also reads the file metadata to see how many bytes each column takes. Everything runs with one command:

git clone https://github.com/BuseKaylan/uns-to-lakehouse.git
cd uns-to-lakehouse
make install
make bench-storage

All results are committed to the repository under benchmarks/results/01_storage_footprint/ as CSV and JSON, together with the Python and library versions that produced them. My numbers come from a 16-core Intel MacBook running Python 3.14 and pyarrow 26. File sizes are identical on any machine, because the data is deterministic. Write times will differ.

Anatomy of one message

Before comparing formats, it helps to look at what is being stored.

Here is one reading as a raw UNS message:

{"topic": "acme-plant/filling-area/line-1/filler/pressure",
 "payload": {"value": 800.53, "unit": "mbar", "timestamp": 1767592800000}}

Of its 134 bytes:

  • 46 are the topic path, which is the same on every pressure message from this machine.
  • 65 are keys, quotes, braces and spaces, which are identical in every message.
  • 13 are the timestamp, and 4 are a unit that never changes.
  • 6 are the measurement itself.

Averaged over the whole day, a message is 137.15 bytes. Raw JSON is not wasteful because JSON is bad. It is wasteful because each message is written to be understood on its own, without knowing what came before. That is exactly right on the wire and exactly wrong on disk.

Round 1: text formats

CSV removes the repeated keys but keeps the repeated topic path, so it only saves about 20%. Gzip is the real step: 21 to 22 times smaller than raw JSON. That shows how much repetition there is to remove.

The catch is that a gzip file is one opaque stream. To answer “what was the average vibration on line 2 between 14:00 and 15:00”, a query engine has to decompress and parse the whole day. Text plus gzip is a good archive format, not a good analytics format.

A note on the write times: the JSON writer is a Python loop that builds one dictionary per row, while CSV and Parquet are written by Arrow’s C++ code. The gap says more about Python vs. C++ than about the formats themselves.

Round 2: columns instead of rows

Parquet stores each column separately. That one change lets every column use the encoding that suits it.

Laid out by column, the hierarchy becomes trivial to compress:

  • A column like machine is just a handful of distinct strings repeated over and over. Parquet stores a small dictionary once (filler, capper, labeler…) and then only small integer indices.
  • A column like event_ts has long runs of the same value, because every sensor publishes in the same second. Runs are encoded once with a count.

Uncompressed Parquet, with no compression codec at all, is already 15 times smaller than JSON. Encoding alone does most of the work. With zstd the file is 29 times smaller, beats gzipped text, and stays fully queryable by column. Writing it took about 0.4 seconds.

Where the bytes go

A file size alone doesn’t say what to fix next. Parquet records the compressed size of every column in its metadata, so we can look inside.

In the zstd file:

  • value takes 3.49 MB of the 5.52 MB total.
  • The two timestamps take 0.81 MB.
  • The five hierarchy columns (area, line, machine, metric, unit) still take 1.21 MB.

That last number looks like an obvious target. The usual advice for time-series data is to sort by series and then by time, which puts each sensor’s history in one stretch. So that is the next experiment.

Surprise 1: sorting made the file bigger

Sorting by area, line, machine, metric, event_ts did exactly what was expected for the strings: the hierarchy columns went from 1.21 MB to 0.02 MB. The values improved as well, from 3.49 MB to 2.51 MB, because neighbouring values now come from the same sensor and look alike.

The file still went from 5.52 MB up to 8.18 MB.

The cost moved to the timestamps:

  • In arrival order, dozens of readings in a row share the same second. The timestamp column is long runs of identical values, which dictionary and run-length encoding handle almost for free.
  • Sorted by sensor, every row has a different timestamp. The dictionary now holds 86,400 distinct seconds, every row needs a 17-bit index into it, and the two timestamp columns grow from 0.81 MB to 5.63 MB.

The fix is to store timestamps the way a sorted column wants to be stored: as differences. Delta encoding (DELTA_BINARY_PACKED in Parquet) keeps the first value and then only the gaps: +1000, +2000, +3000 milliseconds. Those gaps fit in a few bits.

The lesson: a sort order is not an optimization on its own. It changes which columns are cheap and which are expensive, and it only pays off when the encodings follow.

Surprise 2: the float encoding that didn’t help

Parquet also offers BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT, an encoding designed for floating-point data. It regroups the bytes of each float so the compressor sees similar bytes next to each other. It is often recommended for sensor measurements.

On this data it made the value column 65% larger: 2.51 MB → 4.13 MB.

The reason is in the data. The simulator rounds to three decimals, the way most PLCs and gateways report, and report-by-exception only publishes when a value moves. As a result there are only 219,174 distinct values among 1.16 million readings. That suits dictionary encoding, which byte-stream-split replaces. On raw high-resolution floats the result could well be the opposite. The result belongs to this data, not to the encoding, and that is exactly why it was measured instead of assumed.

Surprise 3: the column that was mostly a copy

The schema carries two timestamps:

  • event_ts: when the value was measured.
  • delivered_ts: when it reached the broker.

They differ only for readings that were buffered during a network outage and forwarded later. That is what store-and-forward means, and the late readings are flagged as historical. In this day that is 22,601 readings, about 2%. For the other 98%, delivered_ts is an exact copy of event_ts, and it still cost 0.57 MB, about 15% of the file.

Storing the delay in milliseconds instead (delay_ms = delivered_ts - event_ts) loses nothing, because the delivery time can always be recomputed. But the column becomes a long run of zeros, broken only by outages, and it shrinks to 0.03 MB.

In this final file, value is 80% of the bytes and event_ts most of the rest. Everything describing where a reading came from costs almost nothing. What remains is mostly the measurements themselves, which is where a storage format should spend its bytes.

The full scoreboard

For 37 signals, the difference is 58 GB a year against 1.1 GB a year. Scaled linearly to a plant with 10,000 signals, it is roughly 15.7 TB against 310 GB. That is the difference between a storage project and a rounding error.

What report-by-exception saves on disk

Report-by-exception publishes a value only when it moves past a deadband, or when a heartbeat interval expires. In this factory, sensors took 2,090,880 samples during the day and published 1,158,046 of them, about 55%.

To see what that is worth on disk, the experiment runs the same day a second time with report-by-exception turned off, and writes both runs as raw JSON and as the best Parquet variant.

In JSON, the saving follows the message count almost exactly, because every message costs the same. In Parquet the saving is smaller, because the readings that report-by-exception drops are exactly the ones that compress best: values that didn’t change, at regular intervals. A good columnar format already removes much of that redundancy on its own.

Report-by-exception still matters, mainly for the broker, the network and every consumer that has to process each message. For storage, the format decision is worth far more than the publishing policy.

What this decides for the table design
  1. Never keep raw JSON as the history. Even untuned Parquet is 15 times smaller and can be queried by column.
  2. Use zstd. On this data it is a third smaller than snappy, at no measurable cost in write time.
  3. Sort by sensor, then time, inside each file. The hierarchy columns become nearly free and the values compress better.
  4. Delta-encode timestamps whenever data is sorted. Without it, sorting makes things worse.
  5. Store the delivery delay, not a second timestamp. The late-data information stays and costs almost nothing.
  6. Measure before tuning float encodings. The “right” encoding depends on resolution and on how often values repeat.
Limitations
  • This is simulated data from one virtual plant, not a real factory. Real signals have more noise, more resolution and more irregular publishing. The relative ordering of the formats should hold, but the exact ratios will not.
  • One day was written as one file. Real ingestion writes many smaller files over time, and each file pays its own overhead. That is a separate problem with its own experiment later in the series.
  • Write times come from one laptop, and they compare a Python JSON writer with Arrow’s native writers.
  • Nothing here includes table-format metadata yet. The numbers are the pure Parquet cost of the data.

The next question follows directly: so far every reading has been one row with one value. Part 4 compares that narrow layout with wide and hybrid tables, where one row holds a whole machine.

The full code, raw results and charts are in the repository: github.com/BuseKaylan/uns-to-lakehouse.

items.title: Why Your LLM Harness Matters More Than You Think
items.summary: When building cutting-edge AI applications, most engineering teams fixate almost entirely on the core model. We spend endless hours debating parameter counts, context window sizes, or benchmark leaderboards. But in production systems, a Large Language Model rarely operates in isolation. It’s wrapped in software code that manages memory, formats prompts, handles external retrieval, and orchestrates tool calls. This surrounding wrapper code is called the harness . Recent research introduced in the paper Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses shows that optimizing this harness — without changing a single parameter inside the frozen language model — can create up to a 6x performance gap on complex tasks. Despite its massive impact, harness engineering has traditionally been a painful process of manual trial and error or weak automated optimizers. Meta-Harness completely flips this paradigm. It uses an autonomous coding agent with full access to a project’s filesystem to systematically diagnose execution errors and rewrite wrapper code on the fly. Model Weights vs. Harness Engineering To understand why automated harness optimization works so well, it helps to separate weight training from software orchestration: Model Weight Training: Modifies internal neural parameters. It demands massive compute clusters, moves slowly, and stays fixed once deployed. Harness Optimization: Keeps the base model completely frozen. Instead, it refines the stateful Python wrapper around it — adjusting prompt routing, external retrieval schemes, memory stores, and verification loops. The main roadblock in automating harness engineering has been how optimization systems learn from failure. Standard prompt and code optimizers act like an unforgiving professor who hands back an exam with only a letter grade or a brief summary at the top. Because a harness runs over long, multi-turn steps, an error made in step one might manifest as a complete failure ten steps down the line. When diagnostic feedback gets squashed into short text summaries or simple numerical scores, the optimizer ends up guessing blindly because it can’t trace errors back to their original root cause. The Power of Uncompressed Trace Logs Traditional optimizers restrict feedback to tiny context windows or brief LLM summaries to keep things lightweight. As detailed in the Meta-Harness paper , this new framework takes the opposite approach by using a filesystem store that logs full, uncompressed execution histories across every attempt. Instead of squeezing a tiny 2,000 to 26,000-token summary into a prompt — which is what legacy optimizers like OPRO, TextGrad, or GEPA do — Meta-Harness opens up a diagnostic surface of up to 10 million tokens per iteration. That is roughly three orders of magnitude more context for troubleshooting. When feedback gets compressed, vital clues vanish. A summary might report: “The task timed out.” But it completely misses the underlying bug — like an intermediate sanity check accidentally resetting a completion flag mid-run. By saving every raw tool call, API request, state change, and system error into structured folders, the optimizing agent can read the exact transcripts, pinpoint the exact breakdown, and write targeted fixes. Inside the Filesystem Optimization Loop Instead of stuffing millions of log tokens directly into a single prompt, Meta-Harness organizes diagnostic records cleanly inside a local directory tree. An LLM coding agent acts as the “Proposer” and navigates this history using standard terminal commands like grep, cat, and diff. Inspect & Propose: The coding agent searches past log histories using command-line tools to form a clear hypothesis, then writes a new candidate Python harness. Evaluate: An automated runner executes the proposed harness over a small, challenging benchmark set to measure real-world performance. Log & Store: The new candidate code, step-by-step execution traces, and evaluation scores are saved into a fresh filesystem folder to inform future runs. Log analysis reveals something fascinating: the proposing agent doesn’t just iterate linearly on its last try. It performs non-Markovian search , actively digging back into candidate folders created days or runs ago. In a typical run, the agent inspects over 80 files per iteration. It spends about 41% of its time reading source code, 40% inspecting raw execution traces, 13% checking helper scripts, and just 6% looking at summary scores. By isolating confounding variables — like distinguishing helpful code changes from harmful prompt rewrites — the agent methodically tests ideas instead of throwing random code at the wall. Real-World Performance Across Benchmarks The empirical results published in the arXiv preprint showcase Meta-Harness across three distinct technical domains, consistently outperforming both manual engineering and existing state-of-the-art optimizers: 1. Online Text Classification Higher Accuracy: Running with GPT-OSS-120B on complex datasets like LawBench and USPTO-50k, the discovered harnesses hit an 48.6% average accuracy . That beats top hand-engineered setups like Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) by 7.7 percentage points . Token Efficiency: It achieved these gains while using 4x fewer context tokens than competing frameworks. Rapid Convergence: It reached peak baseline performance in just 4 evaluations , converging 10x faster than traditional prompt optimizers. The Draft-Verification Trick: The system discovered a clever two-stage harness logic on its own. Stage 1 generates an initial draft label using the top 5 memory matches. Stage 2 re-queries memory for 5 confirmers (matching the draft) and 5 challengers (differing labels), forcing the model to explicitly evaluate counterexamples before locking in its answer. 2. Retrieval-Augmented Math Reasoning Emergent Routing: Across a corpus of 535,000 math problems, Meta-Harness evolved a compact four-route retrieval system. It automatically categorizes incoming queries into specialized subjects (Combinatorics, Geometry, Number Theory, and Algebra) using a custom tokenizer that preserves LaTeX math formatting. Olympiad-Level Scaling: On 200 hard IMO-level problems, the discovered harness boosted accuracy by 4.7 percentage points over non-retrieval baselines across five different models (including GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Gemini-3-Flash). Zero-Shot Transfer: Remarkably, the retrieval architecture was optimized once on a single model and transferred seamlessly to four other models without needing any retraining. 3. Agentic Coding on TerminalBench-2 Leaderboard Top Spot: On TerminalBench-2 (a suite of 89 complex command-line tasks), Meta-Harness discovered a wrapper that ranked #1 among all Claude Haiku 4.5 agents (37.6% pass rate) and #2 among Opus 4.6 agents (76.4% pass rate). Environment Bootstrapping: The agent figured out that running a single compound shell command before turn 1 — gathering working directories, environment variables, installed compilers, and memory limits eliminated 2 to 4 wasted exploratory turns per task, saving critical turn budgets. Takeaways for AI Developers If you’re building production AI tools, there are three key lessons to take from this research: Focus on the Harness: The software wrapper around your model often yields far larger gains than tweaking basic prompt templates. Keep the Raw Diagnostics: Don’t throw away execution logs or rely solely on summary scores. Full execution traces are where the clues live for fixing long-horizon bugs. Give Agents File Access: Rather than cramming long conversation histories into context prompts, store execution logs in a local directory and give your agent terminal tools (grep, cat) so it can inspect its own history when troubleshooting. For a full deep dive into the methodology, experimental setups, and code representations, check out the complete paper on arXiv (2603.28052) . When building cutting-edge AI applications, most engineering teams fixate almost entirely on the core model. We spend endless hours debating parameter counts, context window sizes, or benchmark leaderboards. But in production systems, a Large Language Model rarely operates in isolation. It’s wrapped in software code that manages memory, formats prompts, handles external retrieval, and orchestrates tool calls.

This surrounding wrapper code is called the harness.

Recent research introduced in the paper Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses shows that optimizing this harness — without changing a single parameter inside the frozen language model — can create up to a 6x performance gap on complex tasks.

Despite its massive impact, harness engineering has traditionally been a painful process of manual trial and error or weak automated optimizers. Meta-Harness completely flips this paradigm. It uses an autonomous coding agent with full access to a project’s filesystem to systematically diagnose execution errors and rewrite wrapper code on the fly.

Model Weights vs. Harness Engineering

To understand why automated harness optimization works so well, it helps to separate weight training from software orchestration:

  • Model Weight Training: Modifies internal neural parameters. It demands massive compute clusters, moves slowly, and stays fixed once deployed.
  • Harness Optimization: Keeps the base model completely frozen. Instead, it refines the stateful Python wrapper around it — adjusting prompt routing, external retrieval schemes, memory stores, and verification loops.

The main roadblock in automating harness engineering has been how optimization systems learn from failure. Standard prompt and code optimizers act like an unforgiving professor who hands back an exam with only a letter grade or a brief summary at the top.

Because a harness runs over long, multi-turn steps, an error made in step one might manifest as a complete failure ten steps down the line. When diagnostic feedback gets squashed into short text summaries or simple numerical scores, the optimizer ends up guessing blindly because it can’t trace errors back to their original root cause.

The Power of Uncompressed Trace Logs

Traditional optimizers restrict feedback to tiny context windows or brief LLM summaries to keep things lightweight. As detailed in the Meta-Harness paper, this new framework takes the opposite approach by using a filesystem store that logs full, uncompressed execution histories across every attempt.

Instead of squeezing a tiny 2,000 to 26,000-token summary into a prompt — which is what legacy optimizers like OPRO, TextGrad, or GEPA do — Meta-Harness opens up a diagnostic surface of up to 10 million tokens per iteration. That is roughly three orders of magnitude more context for troubleshooting.

When feedback gets compressed, vital clues vanish. A summary might report: “The task timed out.” But it completely misses the underlying bug — like an intermediate sanity check accidentally resetting a completion flag mid-run. By saving every raw tool call, API request, state change, and system error into structured folders, the optimizing agent can read the exact transcripts, pinpoint the exact breakdown, and write targeted fixes.

Inside the Filesystem Optimization Loop

Instead of stuffing millions of log tokens directly into a single prompt, Meta-Harness organizes diagnostic records cleanly inside a local directory tree. An LLM coding agent acts as the “Proposer” and navigates this history using standard terminal commands like grep, cat, and diff.

  1. Inspect & Propose: The coding agent searches past log histories using command-line tools to form a clear hypothesis, then writes a new candidate Python harness.
  2. Evaluate: An automated runner executes the proposed harness over a small, challenging benchmark set to measure real-world performance.
  3. Log & Store: The new candidate code, step-by-step execution traces, and evaluation scores are saved into a fresh filesystem folder to inform future runs.

Log analysis reveals something fascinating: the proposing agent doesn’t just iterate linearly on its last try. It performs non-Markovian search, actively digging back into candidate folders created days or runs ago.

In a typical run, the agent inspects over 80 files per iteration. It spends about 41% of its time reading source code, 40% inspecting raw execution traces, 13% checking helper scripts, and just 6% looking at summary scores. By isolating confounding variables — like distinguishing helpful code changes from harmful prompt rewrites — the agent methodically tests ideas instead of throwing random code at the wall.

Real-World Performance Across Benchmarks

The empirical results published in the arXiv preprint showcase Meta-Harness across three distinct technical domains, consistently outperforming both manual engineering and existing state-of-the-art optimizers:

1. Online Text Classification
  • Higher Accuracy: Running with GPT-OSS-120B on complex datasets like LawBench and USPTO-50k, the discovered harnesses hit an 48.6% average accuracy. That beats top hand-engineered setups like Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) by 7.7 percentage points.
  • Token Efficiency: It achieved these gains while using 4x fewer context tokens than competing frameworks.
  • Rapid Convergence: It reached peak baseline performance in just 4 evaluations, converging 10x faster than traditional prompt optimizers.
  • The Draft-Verification Trick: The system discovered a clever two-stage harness logic on its own. Stage 1 generates an initial draft label using the top 5 memory matches. Stage 2 re-queries memory for 5 confirmers (matching the draft) and 5 challengers (differing labels), forcing the model to explicitly evaluate counterexamples before locking in its answer.
2. Retrieval-Augmented Math Reasoning
  • Emergent Routing: Across a corpus of 535,000 math problems, Meta-Harness evolved a compact four-route retrieval system. It automatically categorizes incoming queries into specialized subjects (Combinatorics, Geometry, Number Theory, and Algebra) using a custom tokenizer that preserves LaTeX math formatting.
  • Olympiad-Level Scaling: On 200 hard IMO-level problems, the discovered harness boosted accuracy by 4.7 percentage points over non-retrieval baselines across five different models (including GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Gemini-3-Flash).
  • Zero-Shot Transfer: Remarkably, the retrieval architecture was optimized once on a single model and transferred seamlessly to four other models without needing any retraining.
3. Agentic Coding on TerminalBench-2
  • Leaderboard Top Spot: On TerminalBench-2 (a suite of 89 complex command-line tasks), Meta-Harness discovered a wrapper that ranked #1 among all Claude Haiku 4.5 agents (37.6% pass rate) and #2 among Opus 4.6 agents (76.4% pass rate).
  • Environment Bootstrapping: The agent figured out that running a single compound shell command before turn 1 — gathering working directories, environment variables, installed compilers, and memory limits eliminated 2 to 4 wasted exploratory turns per task, saving critical turn budgets.
Takeaways for AI Developers

If you’re building production AI tools, there are three key lessons to take from this research:

  1. Focus on the Harness: The software wrapper around your model often yields far larger gains than tweaking basic prompt templates.
  2. Keep the Raw Diagnostics: Don’t throw away execution logs or rely solely on summary scores. Full execution traces are where the clues live for fixing long-horizon bugs.
  3. Give Agents File Access: Rather than cramming long conversation histories into context prompts, store execution logs in a local directory and give your agent terminal tools (grep, cat) so it can inspect its own history when troubleshooting.

For a full deep dive into the methodology, experimental setups, and code representations, check out the complete paper on arXiv (2603.28052).

items.summary_html:
Nous Research has released Arete-27B, a supervised fine-tune of Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-27B. Arete-27B is a 27B open-weight model that strips Chinese state framing from Qwen’s answers. On Nous’s own 803-prompt eval, answers containing propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Developers get Qwen-class agentic skill without state-aligned answers. The weights, eval and training data are all public.

TL;DR
  • Size: 27B dense parameters (all active). Trained at 64k context. Base Qwen3.8-27B supports 262,144 tokens natively.
  • Runs on: BF16 weights are 53.81 GB. A community Q4_K_M quant is 17.20 GB, sized for 24 GB consumer GPUs.
  • Performance: Capability unchanged on the benchmarks Nous ran; political framing now matches Western models.
  • Best: Propaganda rate 0.9%, down from 22% for base Qwen3.8-27B.
  • Worst: Fact score 2.98 of 5; 216 of 803 answers still score 0.
What is Arete-27B?

Arete-27B is Qwen3.8-27B after supervised fine-tuning only. Nous used no RL, no preference optimization and no architecture changes. The license is Apache 2.0, matching the base model.

Nous team states that it saw refusals, deflections and CCP-framed answers on sensitive topics in the base model. It picked Qwen3.8-27B because it was the most capable local model and showed the target behavior.

How was Arete-27B trained?

The teacher was Inkling, an open model from Thinking Machines. Nous chose an open teacher to avoid terms-of-use limits on distillation. It rejected Nemotron 3 Ultra after finding a checkered record on China topics.

Training covered about 52.8 million tokens at 64k context, without sequence packing. The run took 2 epochs and 1,202 steps at batch size 48. It used AdamW, a 1e-5 peak learning rate and tensor parallel 4.

All language-model weights were trained. The vision encoder stayed frozen, since the data is text-only. The multi-token-prediction head was disabled.

The released arete-data-pairs set holds 34,878 prompts across 7 topics. Each prompt has both an Inkling answer and a Qwen answer. 29,236 accepted teacher answers form the SFT split.

How does the propaganda eval work?

The Propaganda_Eval set has 803 prompts across 7 value categories. These include freedom of expression, state ideology, data privacy and democracy. Each prompt carries 2 to 4 required facts from a cited source.

A Grok 4.7 judge grades two things separately:

  • Fact mean (0 to 5): how many required facts the answer states. One opposed fact scores 0.
  • Any propaganda: share of answers that adopt the state’s account as their own.

The judge must quote the exact phrase to flag propaganda. Nous removed every training prompt that overlapped the eval. The eval is MIT licensed and includes grading scripts.

&

What do the benchmarks show?

On the model card page, Arete-27B raised fact mean from 2.32 to 2.98. Propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Answers scoring 0 dropped from 359 to 216 of 803.

The biggest change came in freedom of expression. Fact score rose from 0.89 to 2.44, and propaganda fell from 60% to 1%.

Capability held on Nous’s tests. Hermes Bench moved from 65.77% to 65.60%, which Nous calls noise. Terminal-Bench-2.1 rose from 67% to 70% in Nous’s harness. Nous does not claim credit for that gain.

How can developers run it?

Weights ship in BF16 on Hugging Face. No hosted inference provider serves the model yet. Community GGUF quants run in llama.cpp, LM Studio and Ollama, from 8.64 GB to 53.81 GB. The GGUF build also includes the image projector.

  • The fix took only 52.8M tokens of plain SFT, no RL.
  • Hermes Bench held at 65.60% versus 65.77% for the base.
  • Fact recall rose to 2.98 of 5 but still trails peers.
  • Weights, eval and training data are open under Apache 2.0 and MIT.
